analysis.investment_thesis: CreditAccess Grameen is a microfinance NBFC — a financial company that the Magic Formula explicitly excludes because leverage is the raw material of the business, making EBIT/EV and ROIC meaningless as computed for non-financials. Beyond the structural exclusion, the underlying business is in acute distress: net profit collapsed 63% from INR 1,446 Cr (FY2024) to INR 531 Cr (FY2025), ROE has fallen to 7.86%, and operating cash flow was negative 4 out of the last 5 years.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 28.4% over 6 years and a large AUM base (~INR 27,679 Cr total assets) confirm scale and distribution reach in underbanked rural markets
Strong promoter holding of 66.3% (CreditAccess India BV) and forward P/E of 13.65x suggest the market expects a sharp recovery in earnings, implying ~INR 1,480 Cr net profit within 12 months
Operating infrastructure, brand, and regulatory relationships in microfinance create meaningful barriers for new entrants to replicate at scale
key_risks: Net profit collapsed 63% in FY2025 (INR 1,446 Cr → INR 531 Cr) driven by rising credit costs in the stressed microfinance sector — asset quality deterioration is the core risk and is sector-wide, not idiosyncratic

Debt/Equity of 2.81 is inherent to the lending model but leaves virtually no buffer if NPA levels rise materially; total debt of INR 20,446 Cr against equity of INR 7,164 Cr means any credit cycle turn amplifies losses
Finance costs growing at 29.4% CAGR (now INR 1,955 Cr annually) while operating income fell 58% YoY (INR 2,157 Cr → INR 907 Cr) shows the spread compression that is destroying profitability
red_flags: Operating cash flow negative in 4 of 5 years (normal for an NBFC growing its loan book, but combined with profit collapse signals fundamental business stress, not just accounting optics)
Magic Formula structural exclusion: financial companies are ineligible — EBIT and capital employed cannot be computed in any meaningful way for a balance-sheet-as-product lending business
ROE of 7.86% is below the cost of equity for a high-risk microfinance lender — the business is currently destroying shareholder value in real terms
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I do not apply the Magic Formula to financial companies — EBIT is not a meaningful concept when interest income is revenue, leverage is the product, and capital requirements are regulatory rather than operational. CreditAccess is excluded on first principles. Setting the methodology aside and looking at the raw business: the sector-wide microfinance stress of FY2025 has been severe. Collections have deteriorated, credit costs have surged, and the profit base has shrunk to levels last seen in FY2020.

The forward P/E of 13.65x is intriguing — it implies the market expects INR ~1,480 Cr in earnings over the next year, nearly a 3x recovery from FY2025. That is a bold assumption requiring both macroeconomic recovery (rural income, monsoons) and specific credit quality stabilisation. For a non-financial business with those characteristics I might assign a watchlist rating; for a financial company that is inherently outside my investable universe, I cannot make that call with confidence. A specialist microfinance analyst or Howard Marks-style distressed credit investor is better equipped here than I am.
